subject: On-prem to VPC transport: peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN - proposal & fallback
messages:
From: Samira Khan <samira.k@acmeanalytics.com>
To: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek@redwood.com>
Date: Sun, 20 Jul 2025 08:15:00 -0700
Subject: Private deploy connectivity ask: traffic patterns & recommended transport

Hi Vivek,

Thanks for the quick intro last week. We're starting the architecture review for our on-prem stack to talk to Redwood Private in our VPCs. Two quick asks:

1) For the kinds of workloads we run (bursting model inference, ~1–3 Gbps peak, lots of small control-plane API calls), what do you recommend between VPC Peering, AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and a site-to-site IPsec VPN?

2) If there's a hybrid approach (e.g., PrivateLink for control, peering for data) — what are the operational tradeoffs and failure modes we should plan for?

I've attached our basic connectivity requirements doc and a rough network diagram. Can you loop in the right folks and suggest a short decision matrix?

Samira
Samira Khan
Lead Platform Engineer, Acme Analytics
netops@acmeanalytics.com

Subject: Re: Private deploy connectivity ask: traffic patterns & recommended transport

Samira — thanks, got the attachments. Looping Kim and Ben to give a consolidated recommendation (architecture + ops).

Initial quick take:
- If you need predictable low-latency data paths at high throughput, peering avoids NAT and transmits traffic directly (lower per-packet overhead) but is cross-account and non-transitive.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints) is strong for control-plane API calls and for stronger isolation (customers don't need route propagation into Redwood VPCs), but it can hit endpoint throughput and ENI limits if you push many parallel connections.
- S2S VPN (IPsec) is the simplest to test quickly and is a good fallback, but it adds NAT/SNAT considerations and higher latency; throughput depends on your on-prem gateway.

Kim / Ben — can you draft a short decision matrix (cost, latency, ops complexity, failure modes) and a recommended hybrid pattern? Samira, we'll include a fallback runbook (zonal/regional failover) and a checklist for MTU/BGP/health checks.

— Vivek
VP, Product Partnerships
Redwood Inference

On Sun, Jul 20, 2025 at 10:02 AM Vivek Kulkarni <vivek@redwood.com> wrote:
> Samira — thanks, got the attachments. Looping Kim and Ben to give a consolidated recommendation (architecture + ops).

Thanks Vivek. Samira — below is a concise engineer-to-engineer breakdown. I tried to keep it implementation-ready.

Quick summary (recommendation):
- Pattern we prefer for production when both low-latency and isolation are required: PrivateLink for control plane (API/auth/telemetry) + VPC Peering for high-throughput inference dataplane inside the same region. Use S2S IPsec as a hardened fallback and for cross-region traffic to avoid cross-region peering complexity.

Decision matrix (short):
- VPC Peering
  - Pros: Full L3 reachability, no ENI/endpoint throttles, lower per-packet CPU overhead (no interface endpoint layer), supports high sustained throughput up to VPC limits.
  - Cons: Non-transitive (Redwood cannot peer your VPC to others on your behalf), cross-account peering requires explicit accept, route table size limits, security groups across peering are isolated (need explicit rules).

- PrivateLink (Interface Endpoint)
  - Pros: Strong isolation (no direct route table propagation), simpler for customers who don't want Redwood subnets in their route tables, granular endpoint policy, integrates well with endpoint services and NACLs.
  - Cons: ENI and per-endpoint throughput limits (start planning around 200–400 Mbps per AZ per endpoint depending on instance type/backing), additional NAT if your on-prem is behind a NAT, costs are per-hour/per-GB, requires ALB/NLB on Redwood side for scaling.

- Site-to-Site IPsec VPN
  - Pros: Fast to proof-of-concept, works across regions and on-prem, can be BGP-enabled for prefix exchange, is useful as an emergency/backhaul path.
  - Cons: Latency/jitter, CPU-bound throughput on customer gateway, rekey/hold-down behavior can cause transient sessions to drop (important for streaming inference).

Operational and failure-mode notes (to plan for):
- SNAT & client IP preservation: PrivateLink often hides original client IPs unless you proxy headers. Peering preserves source IPs but be mindful of firewall rules. If you need per-request IP logging for auditing, prefer peering + flow logs or place a pass-through proxy.
- MTU: IPsec tunnels often require a reduced MTU (typically 1400–1420) — run path MTU tests for your inference payloads. Large embedded payloads can fragment and increase tail latency.
- HA & autoscaling: PrivateLink requires multi-AZ endpoints and scaling on the NLB/target side. For peering, ensure both sides have sufficient ENI/Bandwidth headroom; document quotas.
- Cross-account automation: We'll provide Terraform snippets for peering accept/creation and for endpoint-service creation so you can coordinate with your infra team.

Concrete recommendation for Acme (given 1–3 Gbps peak, many small requests):
- Primary: VPC Peering inside the region for data-plane (inference traffic). Reason: throughput and preserved client IPs.
- Control plane: PrivateLink for auth and billing telemetry (reduces attack surface and simplifies customer routing).
- Fallback: Two S2S tunnels to different on-prem gateways with BGP for failover (advertise a /24 from your side, prefer higher local-preference for peering route).

I'll attach a small transport matrix CSV (rows: peering/privateLink/vpn; columns: cost/latency/throughput/ops/failure-mode) and a sample Terraform snippet.

— Kimberly
Principal Cloud Systems Engineer, Redwood Inference

Kimberly / Vivek / Samira — operational checklist and runbook notes (short):

1) Pilot & Canary
- Start with S2S VPN to validate traffic patterns and MTU/latency. Keep peering off until you've exercised traffic (so you don't accidentally blackhole).
- Canary route: route 10% of traffic via peering once BGP/route tables are in place, measure p99 latency for 24–72h.

2) Quotas & limits
- Verify account VPC peering limits, route table entry limits, and ENI quotas. Ask your cloud team to raise interface endpoint quotas if you go PrivateLink-heavy.

3) Tests to run during pilot
- MTU path test (ping with DF), TCP bulk throughput (iperf), small request tail-latency sampling (scripted load), and session rekey tolerance tests for VPN.

4) Monitoring & Alerts
- Redwood will expose health endpoints; we recommend subscribing to flow logs (S3 + Athena) and push them into a shared logging project. Alert on: increased retransmits, BGP flap counts, increased SNAT table utilization.

5) Rollback plan
- If peering introduces unexpected route conflicts, withdraw peering and shift traffic back to PrivateLink + VPN; have a scripted route update ready.

6) Security & compliance
- Use mutual TLS between control-plane services. If customer requires client IPs for audit logs, add X-Forwarded-For header on ingress proxies or choose peering for data-plane.

I'll prepare a small runbook doc with commands and play-by-play for cutover and rollback.

— Ben Carter
Senior Reliability Engineer, Redwood Inference
